field_rule: Texas cupgrass: separate hair-FRINGE true LIGULE from hairy culm nodes; inspect the little CUP/RING just under a fallen spikelet (reduced lower glume fused to callus); check 4–10 upright fuzzy one-sided racemes and attached paired 3.6–4.2 mm spikelets. Do not certify from a fuzzy flowering head alone.

ligule.source: Kew POWO / GrassBase Eriochloa sericea; Texas A&M Plants of Texas Rangelands
ligule.reference: Dense ring/fringe of straight hairs at inner blade/sheath junction; this is a true hair ligule, not a ciliate papery membrane, independently attested.

diagnostic_checks.look: Examine the ringlike CUP beneath the falling spikelet
diagnostic_checks.check: The cup of Texas cupgrass is a globose CALLUS/cupule representing the lowest rachilla internode with the reduced, fused lower glume, directly below the spikelet. After spikelets fall, little cup rings may remain at their points of attachment.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Signalgrasses have developed lower glumes but do not create this same rounded ring/cup beneath each fuzzy spikelet.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase plus Texas A&M regionally checked; actual empty attachment photo pending

diagnostic_checks.check: Texas A&M and Kew both describe a DENSE FRINGE/RING of straight hairs at the inside blade–sheath junction, rather than a distinct papery membranous flap. Distinguish it from hairy culm nodes.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Paspalum flowering heads can also have one-sided racemes but usually membranous inner ligules.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Two independent regional/GrassBase source checks; current source photo has not been validated for collar

diagnostic_checks.look: Count the fuzzy racemes and inspect actual fertile spikelets
diagnostic_checks.check: Usually 4–10 short, erect unilateral racemes about 1.5–3 cm; spikelets PAIRED, around 3.6–4.2 mm, ovate and covered with hairs; five-veined upper glume and five-veined lower sterile lemma. A perennial rooted TUFT has no long runners.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Brownseed signalgrass has smaller ~2.4–3 mm spikelets and a different developed lower glume, and Vaseygrass has many longer racemes.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase description; need two-face floral closeup and rooted perennial base

diagnostic_review.note: Taxon-source anatomical prompts, not confirmed local specimen dissection or verified exact diagnostic photograph.

diagnostic_checks.look: Locate the short-lived root base and narrow crowded head
diagnostic_checks.check: Sixweeks fescue is a short-lived annual historically called Vulpia octoflora, with narrow contracted panicles commonly only about 1–20 cm and appressed branches; crown should lack perennial regrowth.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Perennial F. versuta usually has a more open panicle; juvenile growth shapes may overlap
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase under Vulpia; regional head character supported

diagnostic_checks.check: GrassBase describes 5–17 florets in narrow 4–10 mm spikelets; a fertile lemma usually around 2.7–6.5 mm with FIVE veins; awns vary widely from ~0.3–6 mm (do not force 'long obvious').
diagnostic_checks.compare: Larger multi-flowered brome spikelets, plus F. versuta perennial structures
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase-backed; local voucher and variety to confirm

diagnostic_checks.look: Look for a minute TRUE ligule
diagnostic_checks.check: A short, hairless membrane roughly 0.5–1 mm, contrasting with the rolled/involute very narrow leaf blades; individual hairs elsewhere on the sheath are not this ligule.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Texas fescue also has a short membrane, so verify growth habit and spikelet details

habit.reference: Rhizomatous wetland grass; foliage and cutting leaf edges can help confirmation.

diagnostic_checks.look: Handle the blade edge carefully for backward-pointing prickles
diagnostic_checks.check: Rice cutgrass has sharply SCABROUS leaf margins that catch when a finger moves toward the leaf base. In wet riparian habitat this is a useful vegetative clue; don't assume every rough wetland grass is Leersia.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Phragmites and other wetland grasses may have rough blades, but their spikelet floral construction differs.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA and wetlands flora support; use noninjurious loupe rather than dragging bare skin

diagnostic_checks.look: Dissect a mature compressed spikelet—both glumes are absent
diagnostic_checks.check: Rice cutgrass has a ONE-FLORET flattened spikelet, normally 3.5–5(6.5) mm, **no glumes**, and a five-veined strongly hairy/rough keel on its hardened lemma; palea nearly equal to lemma.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Paspalum may lack LOWER glume but has an UPPER glume and typically two florets, so 'glumeless' has different meaning here.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA plus USDA wetland guide; true lemma/palea photo needs 10–20×

diagnostic_checks.look: Search upper leaf sheaths for a hidden panicle
diagnostic_checks.check: Perennial, rhizomatous rice cutgrass can have an OPEN 10–20 cm panicle or reduced CLEISTOGAMOUS (selfing) panicles partly/fully enclosed in upper leaf sheaths. Check rooted runners and hidden flowers before marking 'no head'.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Green sprangletop hides similar selfing structures in LOWER leaf sheaths, but has multiple florets and glumes; they differ substantially.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA wetland biology; upper-sheath observation and root connection pending

diagnostic_review.note: Taxon-source anatomical prompts, not confirmed local specimen dissection or verified exact diagnostic photograph.
